notes.liri-wa: For places and things: Hospitali iko wapi? Where is the hospital?
notes.karibu-na: The same karibu as “welcome”: it means close.
notes.yimirira: Also what you say to the driver when you want to get off: Simama hapa!
notes.awaka: Nyumba is house; nyumbani is at home, to home.
notes.matatu: Matatu in Kenya and Uganda, daladala in Tanzania.
notes.ekyalo: Plural: vijiji. Kijijini: in the village.

guidebook.intro: Getting around East Africa means minibuses with names painted on the back, boda bodas weaving through traffic, and asking directions from whoever is nearest.

tips.title: Iko wapi?
body: To ask where a place or thing is, put **iko wapi?** after it: **Benki iko wapi?** (where is the bank?). The answer uses **iko** too: **Iko pale** (it’s over there).
Strictly, **iko** changes with the noun’s class (**Msikiti uko wapi?**), but **iko** is understood everywhere and is what you’ll hear on the street.

tips.title: Ni-na-: I am …ing
body: Swahili verbs are built from pieces. **Ni-na-enda** is **ni** (I) + **na** (now, present) + **enda** (go): “I am going”. Swap the first piece for “you”: **u-na-enda** (you are going).
Add **-ni** to a place to mean “at” or “to” it: **shule** → **shuleni** (to school), **kazi** → **kazini** (to work), **nyumba** → **nyumbani** (home).

culture.title: Matatu, daladala, boda boda
body: Shared minibuses are called **matatu** in Kenya and Uganda and **daladala** in Tanzania. Motorbike taxis are **boda boda** (from “border to border”) or **piki piki**. Agree on the **nauli** (fare) before you set off, and say **Simama hapa!** when you want to get off.
